overview.text: Dental enamel is the hard, mineral-rich outer covering of a tooth’s crown, the visible part above the gum, and is described as the hardest substance in the body. It consists of tightly arranged mineral rods, with calcium hydroxyapatite as its principal mineral. Despite its hardness, enamel can lose minerals: acids produced when mouth bacteria process sugars and starches dissolve its mineral structure. Saliva helps neutralize acids and supplies minerals for remineralization, while fluoride promotes that repair and makes enamel more resistant to acid. When mineral loss repeatedly exceeds repair, early weakened areas can progress toward cavities.

key_facts.text: Enamel covers the crown of a tooth; directly beneath it is dentin.
Enamel is described as the hardest substance in the body and is organized into tiny mineral rods.
Calcium hydroxyapatite is a principal mineral structure in enamel.
Acids made by oral bacteria can dissolve enamel minerals; repeated mineral loss can lead to cavities.
Saliva supports remineralization, and fluoride helps strengthen enamel’s resistance to acid.
